articles.title: Missouri has waited months for Ahmad Hardy. That wait may be ending
articles.summary: Last year's SEC top rusher Ahmad Hardy is expected to return for Missouri vs Arkansas, months after the star RB sustained a gunshot wound to his leg.
articles.body:
Ahmad Hardy's comeback appears to be here.

After months of uncertainty following a gunshot wound to his leg , the Missouri star running back is expected to make his season debut on Halloween against Arkansas, ESPN's Pete Thamel reported Oct. 29 .

Hardy was shot in Laurel, Mississippi, in May , putting his return to football in doubt. He won't start against Arkansas, according to Thamel, but is expected to receive a "handful of carries" as Missouri eases him back into action ahead of its Nov. 7 matchup with Texas.

That's a significant development after coach Eli Drinkwitz offered little clarity Monday about when Hardy might return.

"I don't know if he'll be back for Arkansas. I don't know if he'll be back for Texas. I don't know if he'll be back for the bowl game. Nobody knows," Drinkwitz siad.

Hardy returned to practice this week, and Drinkwitz had stated previously Hardy needs a two-week ramp-up period before returning to game action after starting practice again.

Nothing is guaranteed until Hardy actually takes the field. But five months after being shot, the SEC's reigning rushing leader appears closer than ever to completing a remarkable comeback.

Hardy's status for Saturday is not confirmed, but according to Thamel he should make his return. Although he won't start, he'll see game action.

Hardy was shot in his home state of Mississippi in May.

He was hit in the leg and got surgery afterwards.

Hardy was projected as one of the SEC's best backs again coming into this season. In his first season with Missouri after transferring from Louisiana-Monroe, he rushed for 1,649 yards and 16 touchdowns on 256 attempts.

Hardy also caught six passes for 22 yards, but did not add to his touchdown total in the passing game.

articles.title: Milwaukee Brewers’ William Contreras becomes subject of an iconic World Series photograph
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers captured their first World Series title on Wednesday, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays to make franchise history. While several players del...
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers captured their first World Series title on Wednesday, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays to make franchise history. While several players delivered memorable performances throughout the championship run, catcher William Contreras ultimately took home the World Series MVP award.

Contreras also found himself at the center of what MLB considers one of the most memorable sports photographs in recent memory. The image captures the emotional moment Milwaukee clinched the championship, showing the catcher on his knees with his arms raised toward the sky in celebration.

The photograph's simplicity makes it even more striking, featuring only Contreras and a lone bat resting beside him. Its composition has drawn comparisons to some of the world's most celebrated works of art, with some suggesting it belongs in the Louvre in Paris alongside the Mona Lisa.

The image also offers an impressive view of Tropicana Field, giving the venue a moment in the spotlight despite the Rays' defeat. As Rodger Sherman pointed out on Bluesky, capturing a shot like this is only possible inside a domed stadium.

"one of the best images in baseball history and you could only take it in a domed venue with prominent rigging all around the ceiling for lights and cameras. big Tropicana Field W," Sherman wrote.

Contreras finished the World Series batting .381, collecting eight hits and driving in four runs. Across the entire postseason, he hit .373 with three home runs and nine RBIs. Sports has always produced unforgettable images, and Getty Images photographer Carmen Mandato can take pride in adding another iconic moment to that history.

articles.title: Russia's international ice hockey ban overturned
articles.summary: The Court of Arbitration for Sport overturns the ban on Russia by ice hockey's global governing body.
articles.body:
The Court of Arbitration for Sport has overturned the ban on Russia by ice hockey's global governing body.

Russia have been suspended from competing in International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) events since the country invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

Earlier this year the IIHF said Russia's teams would remain excluded after a review by the organisation's council.

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation (RIHF) appealed that decision to Cas, which has upheld it following an in-person hearing at its headquarters in Lausanne, Switzerland.

A statement from Cas said that arguments made by the IIHF "citing safety, security and other concerns" were "not supported by sufficient evidence".

Russia are now set to be part of IIHF events in the 2026-27 season, including the men's and women's World Championships.

It is unclear what restrictions, if any, will be in place in relation to flags, clothing and the playing of the national anthem.

Individual athletes from Russia were allowed to compete at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Italy under a neutral flag, although not in ice hockey.

The IIHF expressed "disappointment" with the ruling.

"The IIHF disagrees with this aspect of the ruling and maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions," they said in a statement.

"While the IIHF respects the authority of Cas and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments."

Ukraine have qualified for next year's men's World Championship, which is scheduled to be held in Germany from 14 to 30 May.

The IIHF said the ruling has not taken into account the material impact of the decision including a review of competition formats, schedules, travel and accommodation arrangements, and safety and security measures.

"Cas does not consider the practical elements which cannot be implemented immediately," it added.

"Changes to participation require extensive coordination with the relevant Member National Associations, organising committees and host authorities."

A statement from the RIHF said it "welcomes the decision" from Cas and they will work with the IIHF to "facilitate the return of Russian teams to competitions".

articles.title: Russia back in ice hockey world championships after sport court ruling
articles.summary: Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned IIHF decisions that excluded Russia from events in the 2026-27 season.
articles.body:
Russia must be allowed to return to the ice hockey world championships, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled, overturning an exclusion in place since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The ruling is a major win for Russia against efforts to bar it from international sport due to the war in Ukraine. Russian President Vladimir Putin is a noted hockey fan who has previously played exhibition games with former stars.

CAS overturned International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) decisions that excluded Russia from events in the 2026-27 season, including the men’s and women’s world championships. Russia also missed the Olympic tournaments this year.

Russia’s return throws into uncertainty how the men’s world championship will work next year in Germany, given that Ukraine has also qualified.

CAS ruling cites lack of evidence on security over Russia

In a brief statement, CAS cited a lack of sufficient evidence to support the IIHF’s security concerns.

CAS said its ruling did not address issues such as whether Russia should be required to play without national symbols as a team of neutral athletes, as in some other Olympic sports, or other “organisational consequences”.

The IIHF expressed disappointment with the ruling and said it “maintains that its decisions were necessary to protect the safety and security of all participants and safeguard the integrity of its competitions”.

“While the IIHF respects the authority of CAS and will act in accordance with its ruling, the outcome does not remove the concerns that informed its assessments.”

Russian Sport Minister Mikhail Degtyarev wrote on the Telegram social media app that CAS “recognised the demands of the Russian Hockey Federation on key points as justified”.

The ruling is an immediate challenge for new IIHF President Franz Reindl, whose home country of Germany hosts the men’s world championship next year.

The chairman of the German ice hockey federation, Frank H Lutz, said on Friday that Germany remains opposed to letting Russia take part and that “allowing Russia in has significant security, political and financial consequences for us as hosts.”

It is not clear how Russia would fit back in, since the draw has already been made.

Adding an extra team would make for uneven groups and an even longer tournament to fit in more games.

Kicking out a qualified team to make way for Russia would risk a backlash, especially if that team is Ukraine. It was last to qualify for the men’s worlds, ending a 20-year wait, and is ranked lowest among the 16 teams currently taking part.

The IIHF signalled “practical arrangements” would be decided after it has assessed the ruling.

Russian return likely to start at world juniors

The first tournament where Russia could return is the men’s world junior championship in Edmonton and Red Deer, Canada, starting on December 26.

Other events covered by the ruling are the women’s world championship in Canada next year and under-18 world championships in 2027 in Minnesota and the Czech Republic.

In the history of the men’s worlds, Russia’s or the Soviet Union’s 27 titles are second only to Canada’s 28. Russia last won the gold medal in 2014.

Since 2022, Russia has organised exhibition games with developmental rosters, mostly against neighbours Belarus and Kazakhstan. The IIHF has also excluded Belarus, citing the same concerns as it did for Russia. There was no mention of Belarus in the CAS ruling on Friday.

articles.title: Panthers fall below .500 after loss against Packers
articles.summary: The Carolina Panthers are below 500 for the first time since week one after the team fell to the Green Bay Packers, 27-19, Thursday night.
articles.body:
The Carolina Panthers are below 500 for the first time since week one after the team fell to the Green Bay Packers, 27-19, Thursday night.

Channel 9 Sports Director Phil Orban and Reporter DaShawn Brown broke down where things went wrong during the primetime game on Channel 9.

It started so well for the Carolina Panthers. They forced a fumble on the opening kickoff of the game, the first of 3 turnovers forced in this game.

They also stopped the run, only allowing 66 yards on the ground.

But there were just too many weak points and injuries to overcome.

Second quarter, Packers deep in their own territory, Jordan Love uncorked one deep downfield. Christian Watson hauled it in for a 53-yard gain. But the concern here is cornerback Will Lee suffering a hamstring injury during the play.

That's four cornerbacks out for the Panthers, Just too much to overcome in this environment against a passing offense this potent.

Late in the half, a Jordan Love pass to a wide-open Matthew Golden put the Panthers down 20 to 10 at the half.

Late in the 4th quarter, the Panthers were down 14 with just over five minutes left in this game. Jalen Coker powered his way into the endzone to bring the Panthers within 8.

"Loved the fight in the group. Didn't expect anything less. The guys kept battling all the way through. Gave us some opportunities at the end, making it a one-score game," Panthers head coach Dave Canales said.

This is now back-to-back losses for the first time this season. It's also the first time they've fallen below 500 since week one.

The good news is they have a mini bye to heal up and get some guys back on the field.

They're next in action a week from Sunday when they host the Denver Broncos at Bank of America Stadium.

articles.title: TCU Preview
articles.summary: Kansas finally won a Big 12 game. Will Jayhawk fans get another treat, or is the trick on us?
articles.body:
Last time out, surprise surprise, Kansas won a Big 12 football game!

It took a fourth-quarter comeback, a touchdown with 73 seconds remaining, and a blocked field goal with 18 seconds left, but the Jayhawks defeated Baylor 25-24 last Saturday.

Now Kansas travels to Fort Worth to face a TCU team that has one of the best defenses in college football, a surprisingly ineffective offense, and the same 3-4 record as KU.

The Horned Frogs have allowed just 4.1 yards per play against Big 12 opponents, held #9 BYU to 216 yards, and surrendered only three passing touchdowns all season.

Meanwhile, Kansas has demonstrated that it can move the football against legitimate Big 12 competition. The Jayhawks have also demonstrated a remarkable ability to make that considerably less useful than it sounds. Turnovers, sacks, and wasted scoring opportunities have been recurring problems, and last week's victory over Baylor required overcoming all three.

Both teams are 1-3 in conference play. Both need a win to keep their bowl hopes alive.

And on Halloween, one of them is going to walk away with a little more hope for November.

Kansas (3-4, 1-3 Big 12) travels to Fort Worth to face TCU (3-4, 1-3) on Saturday, October 31, at Amon G. Carter Stadium. Kickoff is scheduled for 2:30 p.m. Central on FS1.

TCU leads the all-time series 27-9-4 and has won five consecutive meetings. KU's last victory over the Horned Frogs came in Lawrence in 2018, a 27-26 thriller that ended when TCU fumbled near the goal line while attempting to score the winning touchdown.

Ah, yes. Our very own butt fumble game . Mark Sanchez ain't got nuthin' on us.

Anyway. The Horned Frogs opened their season with a 15-10 loss to North Carolina in Dublin, Ireland. They followed that with victories over Grambling State and Arkansas State before losing to UCF and #9 BYU. TCU then defeated Baylor 17-6 before falling 24-20 to West Virginia last Saturday.

As mentioned above, Kansas defeated Baylor 25-24 last week. The Jayhawks are trying to win consecutive conference games for the first time this season. TCU, meanwhile, is trying to avoid falling to 1-4 in Big 12 play despite having one of the nation's stingiest defenses.

Let's begin with the most obvious problem Kansas faces Saturday. TCU's defense is legitimately excellent. For the K-State fans reading this (and I know you are), that means they're really, really good.

The stats don't lie, and they don't look impressive just because the Horned Frogs have played Grambling State and Arkansas State. Through four Big 12 games, TCU has allowed approximately 4.1 yards per play. The Horned Frogs held #9 BYU to 216 yards and 17 points, and Baylor managed just six points.

For comparison, Kansas gained 421 yards against Baylor last Saturday, but needed 86 plays to do it. That's just 4.9 yards per play, considerably less impressive than the total yardage suggests. The Jayhawks also rushed for 209 yards on 56 attempts, an average of only 3.7 yards per carry. Dylan Edwards accounted for 156 of those yards, but needed 30 carries to get there.

None of that is meant to diminish KU's comeback victory. But it illustrates the difference between gaining yards through efficiency and gaining them by running a whole bunch of plays.

And TCU's defense is designed to make both difficult.

The Horned Frogs are allowing just 3.1 yards per rushing attempt, while opposing quarterbacks have completed only 52.9% of their passes. TCU also allows fewer than one-third of opposing third-down attempts to be converted. Kansas has demonstrated that it can run the football effectively, particularly when Edwards finds some space. But the Jayhawks have also struggled when defenses force Marshall into obvious passing situations.

Against Baylor, Marshall completed 17 of 30 passes for 212 yards, averaging 7.1 yards per attempt. That's respectable, but he also threw two interceptions and was sacked five times. That's a concerning combination against a defense that has been particularly effective at limiting passing opportunities.

The Jayhawks will need to establish something on the ground, but simply handing Edwards the ball 30 times probably isn't going to be sufficient. Marshall will need to contribute both as a passer and a runner, and Kansas will have to avoid putting itself in third-and-long situations. (At least act like you've never heard me say that before.)

The good news is that Kansas has enough offensive talent to challenge this defense.

The bad news is that TCU has demonstrated it can make considerably better offenses than KU look pretty ordinary.

Can Kansas pressure the quarterback? TCU quarterback Jaden Craig has been productive this season, completing 67.5% of his passes for 2,066 yards, 11 touchdowns, and six interceptions.

But perhaps the more interesting number is 20, which is how many sacks TCU has allowed through seven games. For an offense that relies heavily on its passing game, allowing that many sacks is a significant problem. And it's one Kansas should be able to exploit.

Leroy Harris III has 11 tackles for loss through seven games, ranking among the national leaders. He's been KU's most disruptive defensive lineman, and his ability to get into the backfield could be particularly important Saturday. It is notable that TCU's rushing attack hasn't provided much support for Craig, either. The Horned Frogs average just 3.3 yards per carry, including sacks, with Jeremy Payne accounting for much of their production.

That means Kansas should have opportunities to create favorable passing situations by limiting the running game.

But that's where things get interesting.

Craig has several legitimate receiving threats. Ed Small leads TCU with 38 receptions for 514 yards, while Jordan Dwyer and Kari Ashley provide additional options. Tight end Ka'Morreun Pimpton has four touchdown receptions, and TCU's tight ends have accounted for seven receiving touchdowns.

The Horned Frogs can hurt a defense in several different ways through the air. Against West Virginia last week, Craig threw for 372 yards, and TCU finished with 484 yards of total offense on 82 plays, an average of 5.9 yards per play. That's a pretty good offensive performance.

Except TCU only scored 20 points (and lost the game).

Kansas needs to find ways to make Craig uncomfortable without giving up the explosive passing plays that have been a problem in recent weeks. If Harris and the defensive front can generate pressure without requiring additional blitzers, the Jayhawks should have opportunities to force mistakes. But if Craig has time to find Small, Ashley, or Pimpton against a secondary that has occasionally struggled in coverage?

KU's defense has been an interesting study this season. The Jayhawks have occasionally been pretty good at preventing opponents from scoring, even when they haven't been particularly effective at preventing them from moving the football.

For example, last week against Baylor, Kansas allowed 358 yards on 66 plays, an average of 5.4 yards per play. That's not an especially impressive defensive performance, but Baylor's offense scored only 17 points. BU's other seven came on a 42-yard interception return. Kansas also held Baylor to 122 rushing yards on 35 carries, or 3.5 yards per attempt. The Bears converted just five of 15 third downs and one of three fourth downs.

And despite getting into position for a potential game-winning field goal, Baylor couldn't finish the job. Obviously, blocking a field goal in the final seconds isn't something Kansas can count on every Saturday. But limiting touchdowns and forcing opponents to settle for field goals is a perfectly reasonable defensive strategy, particularly against an offense that has struggled to finish drives.

And TCU has certainly struggled in that department.

Against UCF, the Horned Frogs gained 343 yards, averaged 5.1 yards per play, and scored just 13 points. Four turnovers didn't help. Against BYU, TCU actually outgained the Cougars on a per-play basis, 4.7 to 3.5, but managed just 10 points. Even in their victory over Baylor, the Horned Frogs averaged 5.0 yards per play and scored only 17 points.

TCU gained 484 yards on 82 plays (5.9 YPP), collected 29 first downs, controlled possession for nearly 38 minutes, and lost 24-20. That's four consecutive Big 12 games in which the Horned Frogs have failed to score more than 20 points, despite averaging approximately 5.2 yards per play.

Moving the football hasn't always been the problem. Doing something useful with it has been.

The Jayhawks absolutely need to limit explosive plays, tackle effectively, and make TCU execute in the red zone. If the Frogs want to drive 70 yards and kick a field goal, fine. Do that three or four times, and we'll see where things stand.

Of course, this strategy works considerably better when the offense scores touchdowns of its own.

Kansas converted just five of 19 third downs against Baylor. That's 26.3%.

Fortunately, Lance Leipold apparently decided that third downs were optional, because the Jayhawks attempted eight fourth-down conversions and succeeded on five of them. That includes Marshall's 34-yard touchdown pass to Nik McMillan on fourth-and-long early in the fourth quarter.

Kansas also overcame two interceptions, five sacks, a missed field goal, and two failed two-point conversions.

There's something admirable about overcoming that many mistakes. There's also something concerning about making that many mistakes in the first place. Against TCU, those wasted opportunities could be considerably more expensive.

The Horned Frogs have allowed opponents to convert just 30.6% of their third downs. They have also limited opponents to three passing touchdowns all season. This is not a defense that is likely to surrender a whole bunch of scoring opportunities. If KU repeatedly finds itself facing third-and-long, gives away possessions with turnovers, or fails to capitalize after moving into scoring position, the Jayhawks may not get enough opportunities to recover.

Fortunately, TCU has its own problems in that department. The Horned Frogs have committed 12 turnovers this season, including six interceptions and six lost fumbles. Against West Virginia, TCU gained 219 more yards than the Mountaineers and still lost by four points.

Both teams have demonstrated that they can gain yards. Both have also demonstrated a remarkable ability to make those yards less valuable than they should be. So, I don't expect Saturday to be a particularly high-scoring affair. I expect both teams to move the football between the 20s, struggle to finish drives, and spend a fair amount of time deciding whether they should attempt a field goal or go for it on fourth down.

And given what we've seen from both teams, I'm not convinced either decision is going to work particularly well.

This could come down to field position, turnovers, and which team manages to turn a couple of scoring opportunities into touchdowns instead of field goals. Or, knowing Kansas football, which team manages to miss fewer field goals.

Either way, I'm expecting a game in which every point matters.

I can see a path to victory for Kansas. TCU has struggled to score against Big 12 opponents, its running game isn't particularly effective, and the Jayhawks have demonstrated that they can move the football against good defenses. But TCU's defense is legitimately excellent, and KU has had enough problems with turnovers, negative plays, and inconsistent execution that expecting offensive fireworks seems foolish.

On the other side, I wouldn't be surprised to see Craig move the football between the 20s, particularly through the air, only to have drives stall in or near the red zone.

I'm expecting a relatively low-scoring game with plenty of field goals. Or field goal attempts. (The total is 46.5 points as of Thursday night — do with that what you will.)

Kansas finally gave us a treat against Baylor last Saturday. But after everything we've watched this season, I'm not convinced the Jayhawks don't have another trick waiting for us in Fort Worth.

I said I'd believe it when I see it. Well, I've seen it once. I've gotta see it again. One victory doesn't erase everything we've watched over the first seven games. Kansas has demonstrated that it can compete with Big 12 opponents, but it hasn't demonstrated that it can consistently beat them. Until that changes, I'm having a difficult time picking the Jayhawks to win on the road against a team with this kind of defense.

I expect Kansas to be competitive. I expect the Jayhawks to have opportunities to win. But I also expect TCU to survive.

The last time Kansas beat TCU in Fort Worth was in 1996, when Glen Mason's Jayhawks defeated the Horned Frogs 52-17. Perhaps the most memorable meeting came in 2017, when #4 TCU embarrassed David Beaty's Jayhawks 43-0. KU finished with 21 yards of total offense, never crossed midfield, and tied the NCAA record with its 44th consecutive road loss.

You read that right. Twenty-one yards. On national television, over the air, on FOX. You didn't even need cable to watch this embarrassment. And, of course, there was the running clock. With severe weather (allegedly) approaching, the coaches agreed to let the clock run continuously for the final 12:49 of the fourth quarter. Beaty went on Hawk Talk a few days later and denied agreeing to the running clock, or that there had even been one.

And then, of course, as mentioned earlier, Beaty nearly blew the game the following year in Lawrence because he didn't know the free kick rule .

Just Kansas football doing Kansas football things.

Although, if TCU wants to give us a running clock with Kansas leading 43-0? I suppose we could discuss it.

articles.title: Ranking Mets' top 5 trade targets for 2026-27 MLB offseason
articles.summary: Drew Rasmussen and Hunter Brown could be among the Mets' most intriguing trade targets this offseason. Here are the top five potential targets, ranked.
articles.body:
There will rightfully be a ton of attention paid to the Mets' options in free agency , with ace left-hander Tarik Skubal potentially at the very top of their list of target s.

But the trade market could be percolating, too.

Shortly after spinning a handful of trade deadline deals this past summer, bringing in a bevy of intriguing prospects while bolstering the Mets' farm system, head of baseball operations David Stearns was not shy about the possibility that some of those recently-acquired prospects could be quickly turned around as part of other deals that help New York.

That doesn't mean the Mets are in a rush to trade any of them, but the infusion of talent into their system likely makes it easier to swing an impact trade or two.

And given New York's plethora of infield options who are close to the majors (including Jefferson Rojas , Mitch Voit , and Émilien Pitre ), it's not outlandish to think Stearns could deal from that relative glut in an effort to improve the team elsewhere -- perhaps in the starting rotation.

With offseason moving and shaking beginning soon, there's every reason to believe there will be a free agent and trade frenzy over the next month with the lockout looming on Dec. 1 when the CBA expires. So the Mets, and every other team, could be in a race to that theoretical deadline.

Here are the five players the Mets should have highest on their list of trade targets, ranked:

Brown is at No. 5 instead of the very top of this list simply because the Astros don't have to be in a rush to trade him. Set to enter his age-28 season in 2027, Brown is under team control via arbitration for two more years. And he's still very inexpensive, expected to make roughly $8 million next season.

But while the Astros can take their time if they so choose, there are a few reasons why dealing Brown this offseason could make sense.

For one, Houston is in a period of transition, currently searching for replacements for outgoing GM Dana Brown and manager Joe Espada . Meanwhile, despite winning the putrid AL West in 2026 with a record of 81-81, the arrow is pointing down for the Astros. Jeremy Peña will be a free agent after 2027, Yordan Alvarez will be a free agent after 2028, the high-priced Carlos Correa can't stay healthy, and Jose Altuve (who will turn 37 years old next May) seems to be running out of gas.

There's also the fact that (with the exception of Altuve) Houston has typically been unable or unwilling to extend its stars, as was the case relatively recently with Gerrit Cole and George Springer , who both walked as free agents.

Adding all of that up, it could be smart for Houston to start retooling for the future.

And if the Astros decide to dangle Brown, who has emerged as a legitimate frontline starter over the last three seasons, the Mets should race to the phone.

Ryan was a buzzy name attached to the Mets last offseason, and could be again this time around.

With Ryan almost certainly set to depart Minnesota via free agency after 2027 (there is a mutual option for 2028 worth $13 million that he would likely only accept if his season is derailed by injury or poor performance), it would behoove the Twins to trade him this offseason.

One thing to note, though, is that the Twins actually became buyers at the 2026 deadline even though they were under .500 (56-57) and 4.0 games back in the mediocre AL Central on Aug. 3. So it's possible they simply roll the dice again in a still-underwhelming division and try to win.

If they don't, Ryan -- who has a 3.79 ERA and 1.08 WHIP with a 10.1 K/9 rate across six big league seasons -- could be one of the most intriguing names on the trade market.

For the Mets, he would be a strong fit in the middle of a rotation that is expected to include Nolan McLean and Christian Scott , and could feature a legitimate ace at the top -- with a Skubal signing a possibility.

When you look at the Mariners' starting rotation depth chart, which features Kirby, Logan Gilbert , Bryan Woo , Kade Anderson , Bryce Miller , and Emerson Hancock , it makes sense why people are looking at Seattle as a potentially big player on the trade market this winter.

As far as Kirby, he has backslid a bit since putting up very strong seasons from 2022 to 2024 in what were his first three years in the league. In 2026, while posting a career-worst 4.33 ERA and 1.39 WHIP, the value of Kirby's stuff also regressed in a big way. But it wasn't due to a loss in velocity, as Kirby's four-seam fastball averaged a career-high 96.7 mph. It also seemingly wasn't an issue with his extension off the mound (something that hampered Freddy Peralta during his time with the Mets).

Kirby's elite command (his walk rates in 2023 and 2024 were 0.9 and 1.1, respectively) has also become simply very good.

But the tools are still there for Kirby, who will earn roughly $10 million in 2027 via arbitration and is under team control through 2028.

An undeniable plus is that Kirby is a New York native who grew up in Rye, so he wouldn't be overwhelmed by the market.

The Rays hold a $20 million option on Rasmussen for the 2027 season, but Tampa has typically traded their higher-priced players ahead of free agency -- as they did recently with Tyler Glasnow and Brandon Lowe . So they could theoretically pick up Rasmussen's option and then deal him.

Perhaps their run to the World Series changes the calculus with Rasmussen. If it doesn't, he would be one of the most sought-after pitchers available.

There will always be some lingering concern about Rasmussen's health given that he has had multiple serious elbow surgeries, including an internal brace procedure that kept him out for most of 2023 and 2024.

But when Rasmussen is healthy, he's one of the best pitchers in the sport. And he's been healthy the last two seasons, throwing a combined 322 regular season innings for the Rays while posting a 2.71 ERA and 0.96 WHIP while striking out 301 batters and allowing just 241 hits.

Rasmussen, who will be entering his age-31 season in 2027, would give the Mets a true ace to slide in atop their rotation.

Yes, every top target is a starting pitcher.

With Gilbert set for free agency after the 2027 season, it's possible the Mariners are more motivated to move him than Kirby.

Gilbert, 29, has been an inning-eating machine for Seattle, tossing 185.2 or more innings four of the last five seasons.

In 2026, he posted a 3.73 ERA and 1.08 WHIP while striking out 205 batters and allowing only 153 hits across 186 innings spanning 32 starts. His advanced metrics were also mostly in the red, including xERA, xBA, chase percentage, and extension.

Like Kirby, Gilbert's arsenal is expansive, though he is especially reliant on his four-seam fastball and slider.

Gilbert might not have quite the upside of Rasmussen, but could be a safer bet due to his mostly clean injury history.

articles.title: What To Watch For: Stanford Cardinal
articles.summary: LOUISVILLE SHOULD LOOK TO ATTACK THE EDGES OF STANFORD’S DEFENSE Stanford is rebuilding their program with a new head coach as well as Andrew Luck as the Gen...
articles.body:
LOUISVILLE SHOULD LOOK TO ATTACK THE EDGES OF STANFORD'S DEFENSE

Stanford is rebuilding their program with a new head coach as well as Andrew Luck as the General Manager. It's going to take some time to get to where they want to be. That shows up on the field with their lack of high-level athletes. It's really noticeable on defense, where they don't have a lot of team speed.

Stanford is giving up more 10+ yard plays than any team in the country, and the Cards should be able to turn those plays into explosives if they can attack the edges of this defense. UofL has more speed than most teams in America, and the only team that Stanford has faced that has a similar profile is Miami. Miami torched Stanford for 549 yards.

STOPPING MICAH FORD IS A MUST FOR THE CARDS

Stanford is on a two-game winning streak, and Micah Ford has played at an insane level in those games. Ford averaged 220 total yards per game while averaging 9 yards per touch. For a big back, he has shown a great ability to make defenders miss in the open field as well as good speed once he gets to the third level of the defense. Ford has been a welcome addition to the passing game with over 100 yards total in those two games. He can do it all for this team.

For the fifth straight week, Louisville's defense will need to stop one single player from taking over the game. They have essentially failed each week, with NC State being the outlier due to an injury. Louisville needs to stuff the run this weekend and force Stanford into long third downs. Getting them off the field and not letting Ford be a key on long drives will allow the Cards to control this game.

LOUISVILLE'S OFFENSIVE LINE CAN REDEEM THEMSELVES

Stanford has six sacks this season, which is the least in the Power Four and third worst in the country among all teams. The small group of teams who are averaging fewer tackles for loss per game in the country includes three who have already fired their defensive coordinator this season.

The Florida State game seemed like a turning point for this offensive line, but Syracuse all but shut down the Louisville running game with 11 tackles for loss. The Orange only had 3 the following week in their biggest win of the season. This offensive line has been objectively bad this season. This game is a great opportunity to truly have a turning point.

I've been writing for this site for over a decade, and I've never struggled so much to find a positive thing to say about an opposing defense. The one good player on this defense will not be playing this weekend. Stanford's offense has been held to one touchdown or fewer in four separate games this season. This isn't meant to knock a rebuilding Stanford program, but there is no excuse for Louisville not to dominate this game coming off a bye week.

Stanford's kicker has a career-long 52-yard field goal. It came against Louisville two years ago to end the game.

Benji Blackburn was not only on the Stanford roster in the 2024 matchup, but he was also a high school teammate of TJ Capers and Daylen Russell.

Stanford's offensive coordinator, Terry Heffernan, was a GA on UofL's staff in 2024.

articles.title: Where do PFF place Jets' Geno Smith, Garrett Wilson on QB-WR ranking?
articles.summary: Here is where PFF put Jets' Geno Smith, Garrett Wilson on QB-WR ranking.
articles.body:
Evaluating a passing game requires looking beyond team totals and individual receiving yards, especially when the New York Jets are involved. We see this all over the league. A quarterback can distribute the ball to several targets with varying degrees of success, and those connections can reveal useful details about an offense's strengths, even when the overall production has been inconsistent.

Pro Football Focus analyst Mark Chichester recently examined those relationships in his ranking of the NFL's top 100 quarterback-receiver pairings . The evaluation offers a different lens for assessing passing production, focusing on how quarterbacks perform when targeting specific receivers rather than judging either player solely on his individual statistics.

For the New York Jets , that perspective matters as Geno Smith and the offense work toward greater consistency. The numbers offer a chance to see how his connections with the team's pass catchers have translated into results, beyond what the final score or a season-long statistical line can tell us.

Geno Smith and Garrett Wilson lead the Jets' pairings

PFF's Week 8 QB-WR partnership report states Smith and Wilson rank 31st with a 118.4 passer rating when the quarterback targets the receiver. The connection has produced 37 completions on 51 targets for 444 yards, three touchdowns and 22 first downs, without an interception.

That production gives the Jets a solid foundation in the passing game, even as the offense searches for ways to maximize Wilson's involvement. The receiver remains one of New York's most important playmakers, and the numbers reflect what the pairing can accomplish when the two connect.

Mason Taylor and Kenyon Sadiq also crack the top 100

The Jets' tight ends also made their mark in Chichester's rankings. Smith's connection with Taylor ranked 57th with a 107.6 passer rating, producing 14 receptions on 18 targets for 117 yards, two touchdowns and six first downs. However, the pairing also recorded an interception.

Smith's connection with Sadiq ranked 98th with an 86.1 passer rating. The rookie tight end caught 16 of 23 targets for 164 yards and a touchdown, while the pairing also recorded an interception and five first downs.

The three rankings show that New York has multiple receiving options capable of contributing to the passing game. Wilson remains the most productive of the three pairings by passer rating, while Taylor's touchdown production and Sadiq's yardage offer different dimensions to the offense.

For the Jets, the next step is turning those individual connections into a more consistent passing attack. With three pairings represented in PFF's top 100, the pieces are producing at different levels. Getting them to contribute together more consistently could help New York find greater offensive balance.

articles.title: Jake Paul scheduled for Dec. 24 return to boxing
articles.summary: Jake Paul looks to deliver on Christmas Eve.
articles.body:
Nearly a year after getting his jaw literally smashed and reassembled, Jake Paul is set to make his boxing return as he's been announced for a December 24 return in Dubai, with his opponent to be announced at a later date. The fight will be Paul's first since Paul stepped into the ring with former heavyweight champion Anthony Joshua , getting stopped in six rounds .

"I've spent years proving people wrong, taking risks and pushing myself against opponents nobody thought I'd face," Paul said in a statement. "Nothing that's happened has changed my belief in myself or what I'm working toward. I'm hungrier than ever and on Thursday, December 24, I'm returning to the ring in Dubai to start the next chapter of my journey."

Dubai is a city that thinks big, breaks boundaries, and doesn't believe in limits. That's exactly the kind of place I want to make my comeback. We've got plenty of names on the list; let's see who signs the contract. Merry Christmas, Dubai. Santa Paul is coming to town, and somebody's getting knocked out."

As it pertains to possible opponents, Paul had recently issued a public list of preferred foes which included Darren Till , Nate Diaz , Conor McGregor , Ryan Garcia , Deontay Wilder , Canelo Alvarez , Gervonta Davis , and more. Current reports suggest Till to be the most likely of those options at the moment.

articles.summary: Former Iowa guard Kate Martin and Unrivaled reached a mutual contract termination.
articles.body:
Despite initially re-signing with Unrivaled on a reported multi-year deal , the league and former Iowa guard Kate Martin have reached a mutual contract termination agreement .

"I'm incredibly grateful to Unrivaled for the opportunity to be part of its first two seasons," Martin said in a statement. "It's been special to help launch a league that continues to elevate women's basketball. While I'm excited about what's on the horizon for me, I'm so thankful for the people, the competition, and the memories I've made in Unrivaled."

Martin's 2026 WNBA season was full of twists and turns, as she played for three different franchises throughout the year. She started the year with the Golden State Valkyries, but was waived on May 7. Shortly after, she joined the Los Angeles Sparks for 17 games before the team waived her in August.

Martin then signed a developmental contract with the Chicago Sky and appeared in two games. Through her three-team journey, Martin averaged 2.6 points on 41.5% shooting in 7.7 minutes per game this past season.

articles.title: Former Iowa women's basketball guard Callie Levin named UNI captain
articles.summary: After transferring to Northern Iowa, former Iowa women's basketball guard Callie Levin has been voted one of the Panthers' team captains.
articles.body:
After transferring to Northern Iowa over the offseason, former Iowa women's basketball guard Callie Levin has been named a Panthers team captain this season .

Voted on by her teammates, Levin was chosen as one of Northern Iowa's three captains.

"I want to be a leader, right from the start on the court," Levin said. "Just being able to have my teammates trust me from the get-go is huge. I love these girls and what we've been able to do this summer, and so yeah, being chosen as a captain is amazing."

Northern Iowa head women's basketball coach Tanya Warren praised Levin.

"The one thing that I know was unanimous is her work ethic, her communication, and how she never, ever, ever changes whether she's scoring or she's not. Her communication is steady," Warren said of Levin's selection.

Levin was a fan favorite during her two seasons at Iowa. During her two seasons in Iowa City, the 5-foot-9 guard from Solon High School appeared in 29 career games, scoring 25 points, grabbing 17 rebounds, dishing 15 assists, and registering nine steals.

Levin will return to Carver-Hawkeye Arena on Nov. 12 as the Panthers take on the Hawkeyes, with tipoff at 7:30 p.m. CT on the Big Ten Network.

articles.body:
Last year in Dec. 2025, Jake Paul suffered a humiliating sixth-round loss to heavyweight Anthony Joshua . Following a strike to the jaw , Paul suffered a knockout loss. He later had to undergo immediate broken-jaw surgery and was indefinitely suspended from boxing.

Now months after the surgery, Paul was finally cleared for his in-ring comeback, and he is now set to box in Dubai on Dec. 24, 2026 in his comeback fight. However, ahead of his fight, his MVP co-founder Nakisa Bidarian appeared for an interview with Sky Sports, where he claimed that Paul could still beat Joshua with proper preparation.

"I was pretty vocal that I didn't want him to do the fight on three weeks' notice," Bidarian said. "He did better than the guy Anthony Joshua fought in July [Prenga] and was not KO'd.

"I don't think it was a massive overshoot; Jake landed quite a few times on AJ [Anthony Joshua], and you saw in July AJ is vulnerable, but it was too fast, not enough prep time. He was cutting weight to fight Gervonta Davis and then suddenly fighting a guy who was 40lbs naturally heavier than him. If Jake had to do that with the right training camp, he'd have a really good shot at beating AJ," he said.

Recently, in another interview with Sun Sport, Bidarian had opened up about Paul's intentions regarding a rematch against Joshua . "Truthfully, he wants to fight Anthony Joshua again. articles.title: 5 things to watch as Jets face Raiders in Week 8 of 2026 NFL season
articles.summary: The Jets host the Raiders in Week 8 of the 2026 NFL season. Here are five things to watch.
articles.body:
The Jets should have been heading into this game with a chance to get back to .500. Instead, they are 2-5, following a demoralizing loss to the Miami Dolphins on Sunday.

In Week 8, they host the 3-4 Las Vegas Raiders, in a game where both teams will be hoping to right the ship.

Smith will face the team he played for last season. On the face of it, this sets up a classic storyline about a player wanting to defeat his former employer, perhaps because he feels they set him up to fail, or because they traded him away in the offseason.

However, this game could set up a different redemption arc involving Smith. The veteran wore out his welcome with Raiders fans, who were disappointed with his play, and reacted badly to him making an obscene gesture towards a fan who was criticizing him last November.

Raiders fans would therefore love to see Las Vegas get one over on Smith and his new team. There could feasibly be Raiders players who have added motivation for similar reasons, too.

When the schedule was announced, some may have circled this game as an opportunity for Jets fans to see what they missed out on in April when the Raiders drafted quarterback Fernando Mendoza ahead of the Jets with the No. 1 pick.

However, Mendoza remains on the bench, as veteran Kirk Cousins has led the league's number four passing offense and thrown a league-high 16 touchdowns.

The story doesn't necessarily have to end there, though. All it would take is an injury or a downturn from Cousins and we could end up getting our first extended look at Mendoza after all.

The Raiders have been one of the better teams at forcing turnovers this season, and they are facing a Jets team that just threw their first two interceptions of the season over the past two games.

Two players in particular stand out as potentially dangerous, so the Jets should be particularly wary of them. One is rookie cornerback Hezekiah Masses , who has a league-high three interceptions. The other is linebacker Nakobe Dean , who is tied for the league lead with three forced fumbles and also has an interception.

The Jets' red zone issues have been well documented. In Week 7, they were better in these situations as they scored three red zone touchdowns -- their first since the Lions game in Week 3. However, their inability to punch the ball in from the one-yard line in the fourth quarter was one of the main things that cost them Sunday's game.

They are not alone in struggling in this area. The Raiders have had the second-highest number of red zone trips in the league but are 29th in conversion percentage. They had one touchdown in five red zone trips in last week's loss to the Rams.

In addition, they gave up a touchdown on all five of the Rams' red zone trips, so their red zone defense has been vulnerable. These issues are the main reason Las Vegas has lost four in a row since an improbable 3-0 start.

Building the offense around Garrett Wilson

Sunday was the second game in a row where Wilson didn't see enough of the ball on offense for the Jets. That comes after he had over 100 yards and a touchdown in their most recent win over the Browns.

Clearly, the Jets need to ensure they are optimizing their offense by making the most of Wilson's abilities. They shouldn't need to get too creative or force the ball to Wilson, but they should seek ways to use their alignment to isolate him in one-on-one situations where targeting him should be a high-percentage option.

It's also worth noting that AD Mitchell and Kenyon Sadiq only had one catch between them against Miami, so Smith has a lot of mouths to feed.

articles.title: Jorge Posada was right about Yankees — and that’s not even the worst of it | Klapisch
articles.summary: The former Yankees catcher put a spotlight on the franchise's malaise.
articles.body:
The Yankees are saying goodbye to the worst month in franchise history, and it goes far beyond the shellacking they took from the Rays in the AL Division Series.

It's what's happened since that says the Yankees are due for a major overhaul.

Here's what the public relations disaster looks like to date:

*Franchise legends Derek Jeter , Paul O'Neill, CC Sabathia and Alex Rodriguez have all savaged the clubhouse culture.

*Owner Hal Steinbrenner took no responsibility for the latest October failure.

*Manager Aaron Boone , who has yet to win a championship in his nine years on the job, said, "I believe we can win with me at the helm. … I think I'm good at my job."

* Jorge Posada , a beloved member of the Core Four, believes he's no longer welcome at spring training .

*Brewers manager Pat Murphy, celebrating the franchise's first world championship on Wednesday, called the Yankees "horses---" and accused them of "playing for [themselves]."

If none of this embarrasses Steinbrenner, then he might as well go into hiding forever. The pointless once-a-year press conferences do nothing but enrage the fan base anyway.

My advice to Steinbrenner is to take the final step and stay away entirely.

But before Steinbrenner vanishes, he should take a closer look at the two most damaging indictments against the Yankees.

Steinbrenner can start by asking why an esteemed champion like Posada believes he's being snubbed.

Second, Steinbrenner should demand to know how the Yankees have fallen so far that a small-market manager like Murphy is comfortable trashing his team, moments after winning the World Series.

Are the Yankees that much of an industry joke? Have the people in charge allowed North America's most iconic franchise to turn into the MLB's laughingstock?

It wasn't that long ago that the Yankees were the industry's most prestigious club. As O'Neill told me earlier this month , "You're the New York Yankees. You're different because of the tradition and because of the name: New York Yankees ."

That history should still mean something — certainly to the current generation. That's why Posada's accusation, which he made during a New York Post podcast, was so shocking.

I don't believe Posada was referring to the front office or to Boone, who personally invites former Yankees to spring training. The franchise itself has made sure to honor Posada over the years. They've retired his No. 20, awarded him a plaque in Monument Park in 2015 and invited him to the 25 th anniversary ceremony for the 1998 team in 2023 and the Sept. 11 memorial event at Yankee Stadium last month.

I reached out to two former Yankees on Thursday, neither of whom wanted to discuss Posada's comments on the record. They consider the matter between the former catcher and the team's hierarchy, pointing out that a number of retired stars, including Tino Martinez, Bernie Williams and Ron Guidry, come to spring training every year.

"If the older guys were a problem, then why are guys like Gator and Tino always in camp?" one former Yankee asked.

When Posada told the Post's Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman, "I don't think they want me there," he was likely referring to the current players.

Although Posada never identified who "they" were, the disconnect between the generations is startling. Other than the uniform, Posada has nothing in common with the present-day Yankees.

He was, and still is, as intense as they are laid back. While Aaron Judge is respectful of ex-Yankees, even he would be considered too even-keeled for the '98 bunch.

I recall what one long-time member of the organization told me over the summer about the evolution of the clubhouse. He'd been around long enough to remember the Joe Torre era — back when "losing really pissed guys off. They hated it.

"But now, when you walk in the room, there's no difference between a good game or bad game," he said. "You would never know they'd just lost by the way they react."

It's possible Posada, as tightly wound as he was during his playing days, might be misreading the calm in the clubhouse. Posada could feel alienated in a room where there's no equivalent to Jeter, O'Neill or Mariano Rivera.

But that's the way baseball has changed in the quarter-century since Posada's prime. The message that trickles down from the front office doesn't demand domination, only emotional balance. Don't overreact.

During the playoffs, a longtime scout told me the best way to evaluate the Yankees is to look for the subtle signs of what drives them.

"Watch them between innings," the scout said. "How many of them run out to their position? How many of them walk? I was shocked."

This is the signature of a team that has no fear of its owner or manager. Steinbrenner's authority has no teeth. Boone's permissiveness enabled Jazz Chisholm's lack of hustle.

The belief around the sport is that the Yankees get away with this by intimidating mediocre teams. They've got the star power, the tradition, the aura, the iconic stadium. But the better clubs know that talent can only take you so far, especially in October.

That's what Murphy was talking about when he bear-hugged Jake Bauers after Game 5 of the World Series.

"You're going to be a rich (expletive)," Murphy told Bauers, who is eligible for free agency. "Just remember when you're on that horses--- Yankees team and you're all playing for yourselves; just remember this is the way we used to do it."

No opposing manager would ever have insulted Torre's Yankees that way, or even Joe Girardi's. I bet Murphy isn't the only manager who feels that way about Boone's Yankees.

It's up to Steinbrenner to ask himself when enough is enough.

articles.summary: El técnico madrileño repasa su nueva aventura en Ámsterdam en una entrevista en 'El Programa de Ortega', además de recordar sus raíces en el Rayo Vallecano y a sus grandes ídolos futbolísticos
articles.body: Día especial para Miguel Ángel Sánchez Muñoz, "Míchel". El entrenador del Ajax de Ámsterdam ha celebra este 30 de octubre su cumpleaños y lo ha hecho recibiendo la felicitación de Radio MARCA, donde ha repasado su presente en los Países Bajos, su trayectoria como futbolista y entrenador y algunos de los recuerdos que han marcado su carrera. Míchel no ha escondido la ilusión que le produce dirigir a uno de los clubes más históricos del fútbol europeo. "Entrenar al Ajax es un privilegio. Coger las riendas de un equipo como este es muy bonito y es histórico", reconoció durante la conversación con Vicente Ortega. El técnico también destacó la importancia de la filosofía que ha acompañado tradicionalmente al conjunto neerlandés, con figuras como Johan Cruyff y Rinus Michels como grandes referentes. Una herencia futbolística que sigue muy presente en el club y que Míchel disfruta especialmente desde su llegada a Ámsterdam. Uno de los momentos más personales de la charla llegó al recordar su etapa como futbolista del Rayo Vallecano. Míchel confirmó que tuvo la oportunidad de irse al Real Madrid, pero decidió quedarse en Vallecas por su sentimiento rayista. "Era muy rayista y le dije a mi padre que querían que fuera a comer con una persona del Madrid que era muy importante. Al final no fui a aquella comida porque dije que me quería quedar en el Rayo", recordó. Y fue rotundo al ser preguntado por si alguna vez se había arrepentido: "No, nunca. Jugar en el Rayo era mi objetivo, mi pasión. Era lo más importante y estoy muy orgulloso de mi carrera". El técnico también mostró su preocupación por la situación institucional que atraviesa el club franjirrojo y defendió a su afición. "La afición del Rayo es la mejor del mundo", afirmó, lamentando que se hable más de los problemas extradeportivos que de los éxitos deportivos recientes del equipo. Uno de los aspectos que más está llamando la atención del entrenador es el talento joven que encuentra en la estructura del Ajax. Míchel destacó el nivel de los futbolistas de 17, 18 y 19 años con los que trabaja y la importancia de mantener la apuesta por la cantera, una de las señas de identidad históricas de la entidad. En lo deportivo, el madrileño reconoció que la exigencia en Ámsterdam es máxima. "La presión es la misma que en el Real Madrid: ganar o ganar", explicó, aunque dejó claro que su manera de entender el fútbol pasa por el trabajo diario, la formación y el crecimiento de sus jugadores. "Me apasiona ayudar al jugador, intentar mejorarle y que llegue a final de temporada y me diga: míster, gracias, porque siento que contigo he crecido", confesó al final de la conversación.

articles.title: Canadiens Prospect Report: Jacob Off To Great Start As New Rocket Coach

articles.body:
The Montreal Canadiens may no longer possess one of the NHL's strongest prospect pools, an expected outcome after graduating so many talented young players in recent years. Even so, the Laval Rocket remain among the AHL's top teams.

This is especially notable given the significant loss the Rocket absorbed last season, when former head coach Pascal Vincent departed for an NHL role with the Seattle Kraken. Turnover is inevitable in the AHL, and while Daniel Jacob had accumulated extensive experience as an assistant across various leagues, he had never held a head-coaching position before his promotion.

Turnover is inevitable in the AHL, and there's no Daniel Jacob absorbed an abundance of coaching experience during his many years spent as an assistant coach in various leagues, but the fact remained that he was yet to be tasked with a head coaching job prior to his promotion.

Yet the Rocket have done far more than tread water. They currently sit atop the North Division with an impressive 7-3-0 record and a +17 goal differential. Jacob has managed this success despite numerous call-ups of key players, including Jacob Fowler, Owen Beck, and David Reinbacher, and without Adam Engstrom and Florian Xhekaj, two skaters who played crucial roles in the lineup over the past two seasons.

Such is life in the AHL, where the only constant is inconsistency. The ability to adapt on the fly is essential, and Jacob has handled that challenge with aplomb in his rookie season as a head coach.

It's unlikely this ranking will hold through the end of the regular season, but as things stand, the Rocket currently host two of the AHL's top point producers .

Making the situation even more intriguing is that rookie defenceman Luke Mittelstadt leads the entire league in scoring with an impressive five goals and 11 assists in 10 games. Newcomer Reilly Walsh has kept close pace, posting a very respectable five goals and eight assists.

In fact, the Rocket's top three point producers were all added to the roster this summer. Sasha Pastujov rounds out the group with six goals and five assists for his new team.

With that in mind, credit for Laval's strong start extends well beyond Jacob, though he certainly deserves significant praise for his work in a challenging situation.

General manager John Sedgwick identified several areas of weakness over the summer and made sure his rookie head coach had the necessary tools to succeed. Running an AHL team may not be glamorous, but it requires a wide range of skills that will one day prove essential for anyone aspiring to the same role in the NHL.

The true test will come in the playoffs, where the Rocket have fallen short of expectations in recent seasons.

That being said, given all the variables at play, it would be hard to argue that the Canadiens' farm team has not opened the season with the focus, intensity, and team-first approach required for success at the AHL level.
